summary_html: Immediate state action to **protect a child in imminent danger**. Federal law (ASFA/IV-E) ties funding to court findings on **reasonable efforts**, and constitutional limits (due process, 4th/14th Amendments) constrain warrantless removals.
authority_html:
- **ASFA / SSA Title IV-E** — reasonable-efforts findings; permanency timelines  
- **CFSR (45 CFR Part 1355)** — federal oversight of removal decision quality  
- **Constitutional constraints** — enforced via §1983 actions; due process & search/seizure jurisprudence (not listed in file but governs practice)

case_law.method: v1.1.0 case-law rebuild: authorities selected per decision point, each opinion retrieved from CourtListener and read; holding and quote taken from the opinion text; independently re-verified before release. Previous keyword-matched Justia listings were removed.

key_cases.holding: In a lead opinion the Court affirmed reversal of a termination because DHS's and the court's repeated failures to notify the father of hearings and to locate, assess and engage him denied him minimal procedural due process.
key_cases.relevance: Once a child is taken into protective custody, both parents acquire notice rights that attach from the preliminary hearing forward.
key_cases.quote: A parent whose parental rights have not been terminated, including one who is not a named respondent, must be notified of and permitted to participate in each hearing

key_cases.holding: The Court held the family court's ex parte and referee proceedings authorizing withdrawal of an infant's life support were fatally defective, that inadequate notice to a respondent is a jurisdictional defect, and it set out the notice, evidentiary and decision-maker standards such a case requires.
key_cases.relevance: Emergency protective custody does not suspend the notice requirements that give the court power over the parent.
key_cases.quote: The absence of this notice to a respondent in a protective proceeding constitutes a jurisdictional defect.

key_cases.court: United States Court of Appeals for the Sixth Circuit
key_cases.holding: The Sixth Circuit held there is no social-worker exception to the Fourth Amendment and that a caseworker may not rely on an accompanying officer to excuse a warrantless home entry, but granted qualified immunity because the right was not yet clearly established in the circuit.
key_cases.relevance: Taking protective custody from inside a home requires the same Fourth Amendment justification that would be required of an officer.
key_cases.quote: We join other circuits in recognizing that Fourth Amendment standards are the same, whether the state actor is a law enforcement officer or a social worker.

key_cases.court: United States Court of Appeals for the Sixth Circuit
key_cases.holding: The Sixth Circuit reversed the denial of qualified immunity to Michigan CPS workers, holding no clearly established law governed a removal that began with the father's express consent and was at most impliedly revoked before a court order issued weeks later.
key_cases.relevance: Protective custody that starts as a consented safety arrangement occupies a legal middle ground where liability is presently uncertain.
key_cases.quote: We find that no clearly established law put the state defendants on notice that they were violating the Bambachs' Fourteenth and Fourth Amendment rights.

key_cases.court: United States Court of Appeals for the Sixth Circuit
key_cases.holding: The Sixth Circuit affirmed summary judgment for the caseworker, holding that parents who voluntarily consent to a safety plan removing their children from the home are not entitled to a pre-deprivation hearing where they never used the plan's stated mechanism to withdraw that consent.
key_cases.relevance: A child moved out of the home under a signed safety plan is not taken into protective custody for due-process purposes so long as the parents' consent continues, which is the legal middle ground between voluntary placement and formal removal.
key_cases.quote: the Smiths needed to explicitly withdraw the consent they explicitly gave, thus requiring Children's Services to either return the children or file a formal complaint against them

key_cases.court: United States Court of Appeals for the Sixth Circuit
key_cases.holding: The Sixth Circuit affirmed the denial of qualified immunity on the Fourteenth Amendment claims, holding that a safety plan excuses the state from affording a parent process only where the parent's consent is voluntary and free of duress, and it reversed on the Fourth Amendment claims while holding prospectively that a social worker needs at least reasonable suspicion of abuse to conduct an in-school interview without a warrant or consent.
key_cases.relevance: Schulkers materially qualifies Smith v Williams-Ash: a plan the parent signs under threat, or repeatedly asks to have lifted, is not the consent that excuses a hearing before the state separates a family.
key_cases.quote: The only exception to this rule is when a parent voluntarily consents to the terms of a safety plan without duress.

state_agency.name: Michigan Department of Health and Human Services

mandatory_reporters: Physicians, dentists, physician's assistants, registered dental hygienists, medical examiners, nurses, and persons licensed to provide emergency medical care — Mich. Comp. Laws § 722.623(1)(a)
Audiologists, psychologists, physical therapists, physical therapist assistants, occupational therapists, and athletic trainers

Marriage and family therapists, licensed professional counselors, social workers, licensed master's social workers, licensed bachelor's social workers, registered social service technicians, and social service technicians
Persons employed in a professional capacity in any office of the friend of the court
School administrators, school counselors, and teachers

MDHHS eligibility specialists, family independence managers, family independence specialists, social services specialists, social work specialists, social work specialist managers, and welfare services specialists — Mich. Comp. Laws § 722.623(1)(b)
Employees of an organization that federal funding statutes, regulations, or contracts would otherwise bar from reporting absent a state mandate — Mich. Comp. Laws § 722.623(1)(c)
Not universal: any other person, including a child, MAY report but is not required to — Mich. Comp. Laws § 722.624
reporting_details: Michigan is not a universal-reporting state: only the professionals and MDHHS employees listed in Mich. Comp. Laws § 722.623(1) must report, and they must report immediately to MDHHS centralized intake by telephone or through the Michigan Online Reporting System. A telephone report must be followed within 72 hours by a written report on form DHS-3200, faxed or emailed to Centralized Intake; a report filed through the online reporting system that contains the information required by Mich. Comp. Laws § 722.623(2) counts as the written report, and MDHHS states that reporting online eliminates the requirement to fill out a DHS-3200 form. Any other person may report voluntarily under Mich. Comp. Laws § 722.624.

timeline_requirements.starts_from: MDHHS centralized intake receives the report
timeline_requirements.consequence_of_miss: Not specified by statute; Mich. Comp. Laws § 722.628(1) requires the department, within 24 hours of receiving a report, to refer it to the prosecuting attorney and local law enforcement or to commence an investigation.
Not specified; MDHHS states CPS has 30 days to complete an investigation unless extenuating circumstances require an extension.
